Reference

This page lists what a sheet can hold, for lookup. Writing a sheet teaches the same language through examples.

Keywords

LineWhat it does
fluid waterSets the fluid for the state lines after it.
state 1 : p = 1 [bar], x = 0Fixes state 1 from two properties and defines p_1, T_1, v_1, u_1, h_1, s_1 and x_1. state 2 (r134a) : … names a fluid of its own.
check V_2 > V_1Compares two expressions after the sheet is solved.
guess T_2 = 400 [K]Sets the value an iteration for T_2 starts from.
plot Ts : 1 -s- 2 -p- 3 -- 1Draws a property diagram of the states named: Ts, Tv, pv, ph or hs. Between two states, -p-, -s-, -T-, -v- and -h- draw a process at constant p, s, T, v or h, and -- a straight line.
function f(a) = 2*a + 1Defines a function on one line.
table d : x [m], y [kg]Starts a table. Its rows of numbers follow on indented lines.
% given valuesA comment. %% at the start of a line begins a section of a published report.

Operators

OperatorMeaning
=An equation: the two sides are equal.
== <= >= < >Comparisons, in check lines.
+ - * /Arithmetic. * and / come before + and -, and operators of one rank work left to right: 8/2/2 is 2.
^A power. A power comes before a minus sign and works right to left: -2^2 is -4, and 2^3^2 is 512.
( )Grouping, and the arguments of a call.
[ ]A unit, after a number: 2 [bar].
;Separates two statements on one line.
,Separates the arguments of a call, the two properties of a state line and the numbers of a table row.
:Follows the label of a state, the name of a table and the diagram of a plot.
1e-4A number in powers of ten, 1 × 10-4. 2.5E3 also works.

Units

QuantityUnits
Masskg g lb (or lbm)
Lengthm cm mm km ft in mile (5280 ft)
Times min h (or hr) day yr (365.25 days)
TemperatureC K F R
ForceN kN lbf
PressurePa kPa MPa bar atm psi (or psia)
EnergyJ kJ MJ Btu kWh
PowerW kW MW hp ton (the ton of refrigeration, 200 Btu/min)
VolumeL gal, and any length cubed, such as m^3
Amount of substancemol kmol lbmol
Electriccurrent A mA; voltage V kV; resistance Ω (or ohm)
Rotationrpm, revolutions per minute as a frequency, 1/(60 s)
No units-, and 1 in a unit such as [1/s]
  1. A unit follows a number in square brackets. Dome holds every value in SI.
  2. Everything after a slash is in the denominator: [kJ/kg·K], [kJ/kg/K] and [kJ/(kg*K)] are all kJ/(kg·K).
  3. A 0 needs no unit, except where it is a temperature, since 0 °C and 0 K differ.
  4. A number without a unit where no equation requires one is a plain number. With W_net = 100 and W_net = mdot*(h_1 - h_2), mdot comes out in s^2/m^2, with a warning.
  5. Dome warns on a result in a unit no usual quantity has when a number written without a unit explains it, through a root too. V in V = sqrt(2*KE/m) with KE = 500 is in 1/kg^0.5.
  6. A result whose unit follows from the units written gets no warning, such as C in C = p_1*V_1^1.3, in kg·m^2.9/s^2.
  7. Amount of substance is a dimension of its own. n = m / M with M in [kg/kmol] is in kmol, or lbmol on an English sheet.
  8. Electric current is a dimension of its own. A volt is a watt per ampere, so E*i is a power and E/i a resistance in Ω.
  9. omega = 2*pi*N with N in [rpm] is an angular speed in rad/s, shown as 1/s: 1000 rpm gives 104.72 1/s.

Functions

CallGives
h(water, p = p_2, s = s_1)A property at a state given by two named properties. The functions are p, T, v, u, h, s, x, cp, cv and rho.
Tsat(water, p = 1 [bar])The saturation temperature. psat(water, T = 100 [C]) is the saturation pressure, 1.0142 bar.
M(nitrogen)The molar mass, here 28.013 kg/kmol.
omega(moistair, p = 1 [atm], T = 25 [C], phi = 0.5)A property of moist air from p and two more properties, here 0.0099257. The functions are omega, phi, T, Twb, Tdp, pv, h, v, s and cp.
interp(d, y, x = 1.5 [m])Column y of table d at x = 1.5 m, by linear interpolation between rows.
integral(e, x, a, b)The integral of the expression e over x from a to b.
der(e, x, c)The derivative of e with respect to x at x = c.
ln(x) log(x)The natural logarithm. log is the same as ln; log10 is the logarithm to base 10.
exp sqrt abse to a power, the square root, the absolute value.
sin cos tan asin acos atanTrigonometry, with angles in radians: sin(pi/2) is 1.
min(a, b, …) max(a, b, …)The least and the greatest of the arguments.
piπ, unless the sheet has a line pi = …, which gives its own value.

Rules in full

Temperatures

  1. A value given in [C] or [F] is a temperature. One given in [K] or [R] is an amount in kelvin, shown in the unit typed. It is a temperature or a change, as the equations use it.
  2. A negative value in [K] or [R], such as dT = -10 [K], is a change.
  3. A sum of temperatures whose coefficients add to 1 is a temperature, as 0.3*T_1 + 0.7*T_2 is. One whose coefficients add to 0 is a change, as T_2 - T_1 is. Dome refuses any other, such as T_1 + T_2.
  4. In a sum or difference, a [K] or [R] number beside a value that is certainly a temperature or certainly a change is a change. So is one beside another sum or difference.
  5. So T_1 + 20 [K] is 20 K above T_1, and T_2 - T_1 - 20 [K] is 20 K less than the rise. With dT = T_2 - T_1, dT + 5 [K] is 5 K more than dT.
  6. The exception is a sum that must be a temperature. That is the T of a state, a T given to a property function, or a side set equal to a certain temperature. There the number is the temperature.
  7. That holds through a name the sum gives, as in T_x = T_2 - T_1 + 300 [K] with T_x the T of a state.
  8. Beside any other value, the number is the other kind of that value. So T_2 = T_1 - 400 [K] after T_1 = 300 [K] makes T_1 a temperature.
  9. Dome reads these classes over the whole sheet at once, so the order of the lines changes none of them.
  10. Dome refuses a bare [C] or [F] number in a sum or difference, since a change typed in °C is the usual slip. In parentheses, (25 [C]) is a temperature.
  11. Dome refuses a temperature in parentheses added to another temperature, as in T_1 + (20 [C]).
  12. Dome refuses a [C] or [F] number set equal to a change. In T_2 - T_1 = 30 [C], a rise of 30 °C is 30 [K].
  13. Dome refuses a change given as the T of a state or of a property function, such as T_x after T_x = T_a - T_b. Read as a temperature, a change of 30 K would be a temperature of 30 K.
  14. Dome refuses 273.15 [K] (or 459.67 [R]) added to a temperature, since it converts [C] and [F] to kelvin as it reads them.
  15. A value is shown in °C only where it is certainly a temperature. These are the T of a state or of a property function, a [C] or [F] number, and a temperature plus or minus a change.
  16. Any other value in the units of temperature is shown in K, such as T_1 from p*v_1 = R*T_1. On an English sheet, °F and °R take the places of °C and K.

Checks and two answers

  1. Dome checks the two sides of a check line for units as it checks an equation's. A check line with an error on it is not evaluated.
  2. A check line chooses between two values of an unknown, or two solutions of equations solved together, when it reads one of their unknowns.
  3. A check line also chooses through a name found from them by one more equation, in which the name enters linearly. With z = 2*x, check z > 5 chooses the solution with x = 3.
  4. A guess line on such a name starts the unknown at the value its equation gives. With z = 2*x, guess z = 6 starts x at 3.
  5. The search for a second answer adds at most a few milliseconds to a solve. It can miss a second answer, so a line with no warning may still have one.

Starting values

An unknown that Dome finds by trying values (see Starting values) starts at the first of these that exists. A name makes no difference to any of them.

  1. The value of its guess line.
  2. In a sweep, a drag or the sweep slider, its value in the run before.
  3. 5 % above the median of the known values in the same units.
  4. The value for its units in the table below.
QuantityStart
Temperature300 K
Change in temperature, where it is certainly one10 K
Pressure1 bar
Specific energy, such as h or u100 kJ/kg
Specific entropy, specific heat, gas constant1 kJ/(kg·K)
Specific volume0.1 m³/kg
Density10 kg/m³
Mass; mass flow rate1 kg; 1 kg/s
Energy; power100 kJ; 100 kW
Entropy; entropy rate1 kJ/K; 1 kW/K
Volume; area; length0.1 m³; 0.01 m²; 1 m
Time; speed; force60 s; 100 m/s; 1 kN
Heat transfer coefficient; heat flux10 W/(m²·K); 1 kW/m²
Amount of substance; its rate1 kmol; 1 kmol/s

Functions

  1. Dome replaces each call with the body, the arguments in place of the parameters, before it solves the sheet.
  2. Units are worked out for each call: function sq(a) = a*a gives 4 m² from sq(2 [m]) and 9 s^2 from sq(3 [s]).
  3. A sheet variable in the body is an input of every call.
  4. A temperature given as an argument is the temperature it names: cp_air(30 [C]) evaluates the body at T = 30 °C.
  5. Dome refuses a call that, written out with every call inside it expanded, has more than 20000 symbols. Each nested call that uses its parameter twice doubles the length.

Tables

  1. A % comment may follow a row or stand on an indented line of its own.
  2. When the column read rises and falls, two keys give the same value, and Dome names both, as for any equation with two answers.
  3. Dome refuses a key that is certainly a change in temperature, given for a column in [C] or [F], such as T_2 - T_1.
  4. A column in [K] or [R] is an amount in kelvin, whatever its name, and is read by value. T = T_1 with T_1 = 27 [C] reads it at 300.15 K.

Integrals and derivatives

  1. A 0 without a unit as a limit takes the units of the other limit: integral(2*x, x, 0, 3 [m]) is 9 m².
  2. In the limits, a name means the sheet's variable. With T = 400 [K], integral(T, T, 300 [K], T) runs to 400 K and gives 35000 K^2.
  3. An integral is found by adaptive Gauss-Kronrod quadrature. Its estimated error is at most 1 part in 1010 of the integral of the absolute value of e.
  4. A table read with x as the key is integrated exactly between its rows.
  5. A derivative is found by central differences extrapolated to a step of zero (Ridders' method), to 1 part in 106 or better.
  6. An expression that cannot be evaluated at some x, such as a property outside its data, is an error that gives that x. So is an expression that is infinite in the range.
  7. A derivative at a kink, where the slopes on the two sides differ, is an error. A phase boundary is such a point.

States and property functions

  1. p and T within 0.15 K of the saturation temperature do not fix a state, since the state may be anywhere on the saturation line.
  2. Dome searches every branch for some pairs: T with h or u, x with v, h, u or s, and h or s with u. A pair that fits two states is reported with both, never one chosen.
  3. x has a value only for a two-phase state. A line that uses x_1 of a state outside the two-phase region gets "x_1 has no value: state 1 is outside the two-phase region".
  4. An unknown that has units only as the input of a property function starts at the value for its units, 300 K for a temperature. Its start never comes from the sheet's other values, so a wet bulb never starts above the dry bulb.
  5. h(n2, T = 298 [K], p = 1 [atm])*M(n2) is 8663.7 kJ/kmol, 5.3 kJ/kmol below the printed molar table.
  6. A figure takes the fluid of the first state in its plot line. Each state of another fluid adds a note to the figure, and its process lines are computed for the figure's fluid.

Moist air

  1. Moist air is CoolProp's humid-air model, a real mixture. At 1 atm, 25 °C and phi = 0.5, omega is 0.42 % above 0.622 pv/(p − pv) with pv = phi pg.
  2. pv is 0.41 to 0.44 % above phi pg from 10 to 30 °C at 1 atm, so check pv_1 == phi_1*p_g fails by that much.
  3. The h and s of the dry air are zero at 0 °C and 1 atm. On an English sheet, h is zero at 0 °F. Dome adds 7.69 Btu/lb to each h of moist air, and takes it from each h given to a moist-air function. Its s is the same on both sheets.
  4. The water in moist air is on the reference of Dome's water states, so a condensate's h(water, T = …, x = 0) enters a balance directly.
  5. Twb is the adiabatic-saturation temperature, taken as the wet bulb. It is the one over liquid water above the triple point of water (0.01 °C), and the one over ice otherwise.
  6. A state near 0 °C can have both wet bulbs. Dome gives one by the rule above, reads a Twb given the same way, and puts a warning on the line naming both.
  7. Tdp is the temperature at which saturated air holds the state's omega. Dry air (omega = 0) has no dew point.
  8. A state with more water vapor than saturated air holds at its temperature is refused for every property. So is a mixture of two streams that would form fog.
  9. An unknown inside a moist-air function whose equation holds only at such a state has no value. The message gives the limit, such as the lowest h at that omega and the dew point.
  10. An unknown humidity ratio given to a moist-air function, with no other start, starts at 0.005.

References

  1. Each fluid's h, u and s count from a reference. Water is on the steam tables, each refrigerant on its own tables, and air and the other ideal gases from 0 K.
  2. Moist air counts its dry air from 0 °C (0 °F on an English sheet) and its water on the steam tables.
  3. Dome carries the reference through the equations as it carries units. A sum carries both operands' references, a product or quotient keeps them, and a difference of two values on one reference carries none.
  4. A chain of sums and differences compares all that it adds with all that it subtracts. So a - b - c compares a with b + c.
  5. A heat capacity times a value that is certainly a temperature counts from 0 K, such as cp_a*T_1 with T_1 = 30 [C]. So does cp_a*(T_1 - 273.15 [K]), whose second factor is a temperature 273.15 K below T_1.
  6. A difference of temperatures carries no reference, as in cp_a*(T_1 - T_0). Nor does a heat capacity times a value given in [K], which may be a change, such as m_w*c_w*T_rise with T_rise = 10 [K].
  7. An unknown h, or one typed in kJ/kg, takes from its equation only the reference the equation still requires. In m_a*h_a1 + m_w*h_w1 = m_a*h_a2 + m_w*h_w2, with the air from h(air, …), h_w2 takes the steam tables', and T(water, h = h_w2, p = …) reads it.
  8. A heat or a work never supplies a reference to close a balance. A property function that reads a variable as its h gives it that fluid's reference first, in the order of the sheet.
  9. An equation or a difference whose two sides are on different references, neither of them none, is an error on its line. So is an h given to a property function on another reference.
  10. A reference belongs to a substance. An equation that takes one substance from two references is an error, whatever the amounts. The pairs are water from the steam tables and water_ig, dry air from h(air, …) and moist air, and R-134a from r134a and r134a_book.
  11. A typed number carries no reference, so an hg typed from a table is not checked.
  12. A dehumidifier written with the vapor from h(water_ig, …) and the condensate from h(water, T = T_2, x = 0) is an error. Write the vapor with h(water, T = …, x = 1).

Sweeps

  1. Sweep values need a unit of the same kind as the input's whenever the input has a unit on the sheet. This holds on an English sheet too. Without a unit, Dome refuses the sweep, and the message gives the line with the sheet's unit.
  2. An input given as a plain number, such as an efficiency, takes plain values.
  3. A range ends at the last value that does not pass stop: 400:30:600 [C] runs from 400 °C to 580 °C. A range with no step, such as 1:5, steps by 1.
  4. A negative step runs downward: 600:-100:400 [C] gives 600, 500 and 400 °C. A list may be separated by commas or spaces.
  5. With two sweep lines, the runs take every value of the variable of the first plot, for each value of the other in turn.
  6. Each run starts its iterations from the values of the run before it. The first run for a new value of the other variable starts from the first run for the value before.
  7. Two variables plotted on one chart get an axis each. Three or more share the two axes by unit.
  8. The legend goes in the corner of the chart that the curves cross least. When every corner covers a curve, a family's legend may go to the right of the plot area.
  9. A family has five line styles and five marker shapes, and six colors. Beyond five values, the styles repeat.
  10. The results table shows five significant digits. Copy data, in the chart's Export menu, and the CSV give eight, after a first line that holds the export's provenance record.
  11. The list of failed runs shows six. A line after them gives the number of the others, which the results table shows in red.

    12. Reports

    1. A section heading the same as the report's title is not printed again.
    2. The inputs table gives each input in the unit it was typed in: m_a = 100 [lb/min] is 100 lb/min.
    3. In a PDF report, a heading stays on the page with the start of what follows it.
    4. A character that the PDF's fonts or LaTeX lack is set as in the equations, so Ẇ is a W with a dot over it. A character with no TeX equivalent, such as ⌘, is printed in DejaVu Serif.
    5. A report with a sweep and the sheet source also gives the sweep's lines, so that the sweep can be run again from it.

    MATLAB scripts

    1. A comment at the end of a sheet line ends the script's line for that line's last statement.
    2. Comment lines stand above the statement they stood above in the sheet.
    3. With MATLAB script chosen in the Publish view, the options for a written report are turned off, and the figures can still be chosen.

    Dome's values and the tables

    1. Dome's properties come from CoolProp's current property equations. The printed tables were computed from earlier equations, so a single value can differ from the table by about 1 kJ/kg.
    2. In parts of the superheated tables, the difference reaches about 5 kJ/kg. Differences between states, and the cycle results built from them, agree more closely.
    3. R-134a differs most, because its differences between states are small. Dome's r134a is the international standard equation (Tillner-Roth and Baehr, 1994), which NIST's published values also use. The textbook's R-134a tables come from an earlier equation (Wilson and Basu, 1988).
    4. r134a's saturated vapor runs 0.8 to 1.2 kJ/kg above the tables from −40 to 48 °C. Its saturated liquid runs low below −10 °C, by up to 2.1 kJ/kg at −40 °C.
    5. Its superheated vapor runs lower as the temperature rises: about 1 kJ/kg low at 60 °C, 2 at 100 °C and 4.6 at 200 °C.
    6. So a heat or work between a saturated state and a hot superheated one can differ from the tables' answer by several percent.
    7. Propane runs up to about 2.5 kJ/kg below its tables near its critical point. Its superheated vapor runs up to 1.6 kJ/kg below them above 100 °C.
    8. r134a_book is R-134a from an equation fitted to the textbook's R-134a tables. Against every row of the tables, SI and English, its saturation pressures are within 0.05 % and its saturation temperatures within 0.03 K.
    9. Its h is within 0.3 kJ/kg of the tables (0.6 kJ/kg for saturated liquid in the English tables), and its s within 0.003 kJ/(kg·K). The R-134a answers of the course's homework solutions agree within 0.34 %.
    10. r134a_book has values only inside the range of the tables: −47.48 to 204.44 °C, up to 39.74 bar. Outside it, Dome refuses the state and names r134a, which covers it.

    The rewrites

    A message that names an exact rewrite has a button that makes it. Dome offers a rewrite only where the sheet passes the units check with it made.

    MessageRewrite
    A [C] or [F] number in a sum or differenceThe unit written [K] or [R], a change; or the number in parentheses, a temperature. In T_1 + 50 [C], only 50 [K] is offered, since (50 [C]) would add two temperatures.
    A temperature converted to kelvin by hand+ 273.15 [K] (or + 459.67 [R]) removed
    A [C] or [F] number given for a change, or added to a temperature in parenthesesThe unit written [K] or [R]
    A number that needs a unitEach unit the message names, written after the number. None for a number added to a temperature, a 0 given for one, or a unit no usual quantity has.
    Two values satisfy an equation, or two solutions satisfy equations solved togetherThe check line the warning names, added below the line
    An equation that repeats the othersThe line removed, when nothing else stands on it; or the equation made a check line
    == in an equation; = in a check line=; ==

    A message whose rewrite would need something the sheet does not say has no button. Two examples are the temperature a change is counted from, and the start of a guess line.

    The Reference pane

    Help › Reference opens the language in short form in a pane beside the current panes. The text below is taken from that pane when this manual is built, so the two always match. Keys are listed as on macOS; on Windows and Linux, Ctrl takes the place of ⌘.

    Statements

    a = b + cEquation. Unknowns may appear on either side; the sheet is solved as a system.
    x = 3; y = 4One statement per line, or separated by semicolons.
    % textComment. %% at the start of a line begins a section in published reports.
    fluid waterFluid for the states that follow: water, r134a, r134a_book (R-134a fitted to the textbook's tables, inside their range: -47.48 to 204.44 °C, up to 39.74 bar), r22, ammonia, propane, air, and the ideal gases nitrogen (n2), oxygen (o2), carbondioxide (co2), carbonmonoxide (co) and water_ig (h2o_ig, water vapor as an ideal gas, h from 0 K, not the steam tables).
    state 1 : p = …, T = …State from two independent properties among p, T, v, u, h, s, x. Defines p_1, T_1, v_1, u_1, h_1, s_1, x_1.
    state 2 (r134a) : …State of a fluid other than the current one. A state line without one takes the current fluid. With states of more than one fluid, the states table shows each state's fluid.
    check a == bComparison evaluated after solving; also <=, >=, <, >. Its two sides are checked for units as an equation's are. A check on a variable chooses between two values that satisfy its equation, or two solutions of equations solved together, also through a name found from them by one equation (r_p in p_2 = 100 [kPa]*r_p).
    guess T_2 = 400 [K]Starting value for a variable found by iteration, in place of the one Dome takes from its units (never from its name). Needed only when Dome reports that a solve could not start or found no solution from its starting values. A guess on a name found by one equation from another unknown (r_p in p_2 = 100 [kPa]*r_p) starts that unknown. It does not choose between two values; a check line does.
    plot Ts : 1 -s- 2 -p- 3Property diagram: Ts, Tv, pv, ph or hs. Tv and pv have v on a logarithmic axis.
    function f(x) = 2*x + 1Function on one line, called as f(a_2) in any equation, state line or check. The body may use the parameters, other functions and the sheet's variables. A function cannot call itself.
    table cp_data : T [K], cp [kJ/kg/K]Table of data: a header line with each column's name and unit, then indented rows of numbers separated by commas. A blank or unindented line ends it. A column in C or F is a temperature; one in K or R is an amount in kelvin, whatever its name.

    Units

    80 [bar]A unit follows a number in brackets. Values are converted to SI internally.
    480 [C]A temperature unit alone (C, K, F, R) is a temperature. A change in temperature is written in K or R: T_1 + 10 [K]. In a sum or difference, a C or F number is written in parentheses: (25 [C]) + dT. Dome works in kelvin, so 273.15 is never added by hand. A name makes no difference: dT = 10 [C] is the temperature 10 °C. A value given in K or R is an amount in kelvin, shown in the unit typed, a temperature or a change as the equations use it.
    T_2 - T_1A difference of two temperatures is a change, shown in K (°R in English units). A temperature plus or minus a change is a temperature. An average such as (T_1 + T_2)/2 is a temperature; T_1 + T_2 used as it stands is refused. A value the equations do not make a temperature for certain, such as T_1 in p*v_1 = R*T_1, is shown in K. A change given as the T of a state or property function is an error.
    T_1 - 20 [C]Refused: a bare C or F number in a sum or difference could be a temperature or a change. Write T_1 - 20 [K] for 20 K below T_1, and T_1 - (20 [C]) for the change from 20 °C. Set equal to a change it is refused too, as in T_2 - T_1 = 30 [C]: a change of 30 °C is 30 [K].
    [kJ/kg·K]Everything after a slash is in the denominator. Also *, ^ and parentheses.
    [kg/kmol]Amount of substance is a dimension of its own: mol, kmol, lbmol. Molar quantities are shown in kmol (lbmol in English units): h_bar = 8669 [kJ/kmol], R_u = 8.314 [kJ/kmol/K].
    [V] [A] [Ω]Electric current is a dimension of its own: V, kV, A, mA, Ω (or ohm). A volt is a watt per ampere, so E*i is a power.
    [rpm]Revolutions per minute, a frequency: omega = 2*pi*N is in rad/s, shown as 1/s. [ton] is the ton of refrigeration (200 Btu/min), [mile] 5280 ft.
    piThe constant π, unless the sheet has a line pi = ….
    unitskg g lb m cm mm ft in mile s min h rpm K C F R N kN lbf Pa kPa MPa bar atm psi J kJ MJ Btu kWh W kW MW hp ton L gal mol kmol lbmol A mA V kV Ω ohm

    Functions

    h(water, p = p_2, s = s_1)Property of a fluid at a state given by two named properties. Also p, T, v, u, s, x, cp, cv, rho. Each input has the units of its property and is checked as on a state line: T = 300 needs a unit.
    Tsat(water, p = 1 [bar])Saturation temperature; psat(water, T = …) is the saturation pressure.
    M(nitrogen)Molar mass of a fluid, in kg/kmol.
    omega(moistair, p = 1 [atm], T = 25 [C], phi = 0.5)Moist air, from p and a pair from T, phi, omega, Twb, Tdp, pv, h; for a pair that does not work, Dome names the pairs that do. Functions: omega (humidity ratio), phi (relative humidity, a fraction), T, Twb (wet bulb), Tdp (dew point), pv (vapor partial pressure), and h, v, s, cp per kg of dry air. Moist air has no state lines. Moist air's h counts its dry air from the psychrometric datum: 0 °C on an SI sheet, 0 °F on an English sheet. Each fluid's h, u and s count from its own reference, carried through the equations like units: water on the steam tables; air (h(air, …), a state of air), the other ideal gases and a heat capacity times an absolute temperature (cp_a*T_1) from 0 K; moist air from its dry air at 0 °C and water on the steam tables; a difference of temperatures from none; an unknown h, or one typed from a table, takes only the reference its equation still requires, so in m_a*h_a1 + m_w*h_w1 = m_a*h_a2 + m_w*h_w2 h_w2 is on the steam tables. An equation that takes water from both the steam tables and water_ig, or dry air from both h(air, …) and moist air, is an error. An equation or a difference whose sides are on different references is an error, so every stream is written one way: every stream with h(moistair, …), or every stream with cp_a*(T - T_0) + omega*h(water, T = …, x = 1); and beside the steam tables a vapor's h is h(water, T = …, x = 1) (h_v = h_g(T)), not h(water_ig, …).
    interp(cp_data, cp, T = T_1)Column cp of a table at T = T_1, by linear interpolation between rows. The key column must increase or decrease throughout, and a key outside the table is an error. A column in C or F holds temperatures, so a key that is a change for certain is an error; a column in K or R is read by value. An unknown may sit in the key.
    integral(C/V^n, V, V_1, V_2)The integral of an expression over a variable of its own, here V from V_1 to V_2. The variable belongs to the call: in the expression its name means the call's variable, never a variable of the sheet, and in the limits the sheet's. It takes the units of its limits, which must be the same, and the integral is in the units of the expression times them. The expression may hold property functions with the variable as an input, functions of the sheet and interp() with it as the key; a limit may be an unknown. Found by adaptive Gauss–Kronrod quadrature to 1 part in 10^10; a value of the variable where the expression is refused or infinite is an error.
    der(h(water, p = p_1, T = T), T, T_1)The derivative of an expression with respect to a variable of its own at a point, here T at T_1, in the units of the expression over those of the variable. The variable belongs to the call, as in integral(). Found by central differences extrapolated to a step of zero (Ridders' method) to 1 part in 10^6 or better; a kink at the point, as at a phase boundary, is an error.
    ln exp sqrt absAlso log10, sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, min, max.

    Plot paths

    -p- -s- -T- -v- -h-Process at constant pressure, entropy, temperature, specific volume or enthalpy. Drawn dashed when that property differs between the two states.
    --Straight line.

    Sweep

    sweep T_3 = 320:20:600 [C]     % start:step:stop, or a list: 5, 7, 9
record eta, x_4
plot eta, x_4 vs T_3

    The swept variable must be an input: a line name = number [unit], or a number written in a state line (x = 0 in state 3 makes x_3 an input).

    sweep r = 2:1:12               % two sweep lines: every combination
sweep k = 1.3, 1.35, 1.4
plot eta vs r                  % one curve for each k

    With two sweep lines each plot is drawn against one of the swept variables, with one curve for each value of the other; there are at most 2000 runs.

    Properties

    CoolProp 7.2.1dev (Helmholtz equations of state; air and five other gases as ideal gases with variable specific heats; moist air from its humid-air model, with h of dry air zero at the psychrometric datum, 0 °C on SI sheets and 0 °F on English sheets). Enthalpy, internal energy and entropy are shifted to named reference states: the steam tables' for water, each refrigerant's own tables', 0 K for the ideal gases. Differences between states, and the cycle results built from them, agree closely with the printed tables; a single value can differ from a printed table by about 1 kJ/kg, and by up to about 5 kJ/kg in parts of the superheated tables. These differences come from CoolProp's property models.

    Keys

    ⌘EnterSolve, with the cursor in the sheet; in the sweep editor, run the sweep
    ⌘.Make the rewrite that the problem at the cursor, or on its line, offers; where it offers more, open them as a choice
    ⌘S, ⌘⇧SSave, save as
    ⌘O, ⌘NOpen, new
    ⌘Z, ⌘⇧ZUndo, redo
    Ctrl+Space, ⌥`Complete a name, unit or fluid, in the sheet or the sweep editor
